types.name: DaoConfig
types.javadoc_summary: Provides DAO-level configuration options that affect query generation and execution behavior.

methods.name: addLimitForSingleQuery
methods.signature: boolean addLimitForSingleQuery() default false
methods.javadoc_summary: Controls whether to automatically add a LIMIT clause (or its database equivalent) to single-result {@link com.landawn.abacus.query.condition.Condition Condition} -based query methods declared by {@code Dao} / {@code CrudDao} , and to the {@code CrudDao} single-value lookups by ID.
methods.returns: {@code true} to auto-append the LIMIT clause to built-in single-result methods, {@code false} (default) otherwise
contract:
When {@code true} , the framework appends:

  • {@code LIMIT 1} for {@code exists(Condition)} , {@code findFirst(...)} , the typed single-value {@code queryForBoolean(...)} through {@code queryForBytes(...)} methods, and the {@code queryForSingleValue(...)} / {@code queryForSingleNonNull(...)} variants
  • {@code LIMIT 2} for {@code findOnlyOne(...)} and the {@code queryForUniqueValue(...)} / {@code queryForUniqueNonNull(...)} variants (so duplicates can still be detected)

The single-value {@code queryForXxx} methods get the limit both in their {@code Condition} form and in the {@code CrudDao} form that looks a value up by ID.

On SQL Server the limit renders as {@code OFFSET/FETCH} , whose grammar requires an {@code ORDER BY} clause, so this best-effort limit is only added when the supplied condition carries one; conditions without {@code ORDER BY} execute unchanged.

Usage Examples: 

 {@code @DaoConfig(addLimitForSingleQuery = true) public interface ProductDao extends CrudDao { // Built-in Condition-based single-result methods receive a limit when needed: // one row for find-first/exists, two rows for duplicate detection in find-only-one.

methods.name: callGenerateIdForInsertIfIdNotSet
methods.signature: boolean callGenerateIdForInsertIfIdNotSet() default false
methods.javadoc_summary: Controls whether to automatically call {@code generateId()} for entity inserts when the ID field is not set or has a default value.
methods.returns: {@code true} to auto-generate IDs for insert operations
contract: Controls whether to automatically call {@code generateId()} for entity inserts when the ID field is not set or has a default value.

This applies to {@code CrudDao.insert(T entity)} and {@code CrudDao.batchInsert(Collection entities)} methods (including the {@code batchSize} overloads), and to their {@code propNamesToInsert} overloads when the ID property is among the properties to insert.
The ID is considered "not set" when it's null or has the default value for its type (0 for numeric types, {@code null} for objects).

The DAO must override {@code generateId()} : the inherited default implementation throws {@code UnsupportedOperationException} , so with this flag enabled an insert of an entity whose ID is not set fails with that exception.

methods.name: callGenerateIdForInsertWithSqlIfIdNotSet
methods.signature: boolean callGenerateIdForInsertWithSqlIfIdNotSet() default false
methods.javadoc_summary: Controls whether to automatically call {@code generateId()} for SQL-based entity inserts when the ID field is not set or has a default value.
methods.returns: {@code true} to auto-generate IDs for SQL-based insert operations
contract: Controls whether to automatically call {@code generateId()} for SQL-based entity inserts when the ID field is not set or has a default value.

Similar to {@link #callGenerateIdForInsertIfIdNotSet()} but for custom SQL inserts; the DAO must likewise override {@code generateId()} , whose inherited default implementation throws {@code UnsupportedOperationException} .

Usage Examples: 

 {@code @DaoConfig(callGenerateIdForInsertWithSqlIfIdNotSet = true) public interface OrderDao extends CrudDao { @Override default Long generateId() { return System.currentTimeMillis(); } default void insertWithAudit(Order order) throws SQLException { String sql = "INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total, created_by) " + "VALUES (:id, :customerId, :total, CURRENT_USER())"; insert(sql, order); // generateId() called if order.id not set } } }

methods.name: allowNullOrDefaultJoinKeys
methods.signature: boolean allowNullOrDefaultJoinKeys() default false
methods.javadoc_summary: Controls whether framework-managed join operations (driven by {@code @JoinedBy} entity annotations) can be performed when the join key value is {@code null} or the type's default value.
methods.returns: {@code true} to allow framework-managed joins when join key values are {@code null} or default; {@code false} (default) to throw an exception in that case
contract: Controls whether framework-managed join operations (driven by {@code @JoinedBy} entity annotations) can be performed when the join key value is {@code null} or the type's default value.
When {@code false} (default), an {@code IllegalArgumentException} is thrown at runtime if a {@code null} or default join key is encountered.
When {@code true} , the join query is executed with the null/default key (typically loading no join entities) instead of raising an error.

Usage Examples: 

 {@code @DaoConfig(allowNullOrDefaultJoinKeys = true) public interface CustomerDao extends CrudDao, CrudJoinEntityHelper { // @JoinedBy-driven joins are allowed even if the join key is null or zero: // loadJoinEntities/loadAllJoinEntities are inherited from CrudJoinEntityHelper.

methods.name: fetchColumnByEntityClassForDatasetQuery
methods.signature: boolean fetchColumnByEntityClassForDatasetQuery() default true
methods.javadoc_summary: Controls the default column-value typing of built-in {@code Dataset} -returning methods (e.g., {@code query(Condition)} , {@code query(Collection<String>, Condition)} ) provided by {@code Dao} / {@code CrudDao} , when individual call sites do not override it with {@link FetchColumnByEntityClass @FetchColumnByEntityClass} .
methods.returns: {@code true} (default) to read entity-mapped columns with the entity property types; {@code false} to read every column with the default column-value mapping
contract: Controls the default column-value typing of built-in {@code Dataset} -returning methods (e.g., {@code query(Condition)} , {@code query(Collection<String>, Condition)} ) provided by {@code Dao} / {@code CrudDao} , when individual call sites do not override it with {@link FetchColumnByEntityClass @FetchColumnByEntityClass} .
When {@code true} (default), columns whose labels match properties of the DAO's target entity class are read with those properties' types.
When {@code false} , every column is read with the default column-value mapping.

types.name: FetchColumnByEntityClass
types.javadoc_summary: Controls whether column values of a {@code Dataset} result are read using the property types of the DAO's entity class.

methods.name: value
methods.signature: boolean value() default true
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies whether column values are read using the property types of the entity class.
methods.returns: {@code true} to read entity-mapped columns with the entity property types, {@code false} to use the default column-value mapping for every column; defaults to {@code true} , and a value declared here overrides the DAO-level {@link DaoConfig#fetchColumnByEntityClassForDatasetQuery()} default
contract:
When {@code true} (default):

  • Columns that match entity properties are read with those properties' types
  • Columns without a matching property are still returned, read with the default mapping
  • {@link PrefixFieldMapping @PrefixFieldMapping} can resolve prefixed column labels to nested properties

When {@code false} :

  • Every column is read with the default column-value mapping
  • {@link PrefixFieldMapping @PrefixFieldMapping} is not supported

In both cases the {@code Dataset} contains every column produced by the SQL, under its SQL column label.

types.name: Handler
types.javadoc_summary: Defines an interceptor handler for DAO methods or entire DAO interfaces.

methods.name: qualifier
methods.signature: String qualifier() default ""
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies a qualifier used to look up a pre-registered handler instance: the name of a {@code static final} {@link Jdbc.Handler} field declared in the DAO interface (or its nested classes), or the qualifier of a handler registered with {@code Jdbc.HandlerFactory} .
methods.returns: the handler qualifier name; empty (default) means resolve a handler by {@link #impl()} instead
contract: When non-empty, the qualifier takes precedence over {@link #impl()} ; the framework resolves the handler by this name instead of instantiating one from the {@code impl} attribute.
This is useful when you want to register a handler instance once (with custom configuration or dependencies) and then reference it from multiple DAO interfaces or methods by name.

Usage Examples: 

 {@code // Register handler instances at startup (e.g., Jdbc.HandlerFactory.register("auditHandler", new AuditHandler(...))) @Handler(qualifier = "auditHandler") public interface ConfigDao extends CrudDao { // The handler registered under "auditHandler" will be applied } }

The qualifier must resolve to a handler instance at DAO initialization time: a {@code static final} field of that name on the DAO (or a nested class of it) is looked up first, then {@code Jdbc.HandlerFactory} .
If neither yields a handler, DAO initialization fails with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

The DAO's own {@link Jdbc.Handler} -typed fields are collected whether or not any qualifier references them, and each must be {@code static final} (automatic for an interface field, but not for one declared in a nested class) with a name unique across the DAO and its nested classes; violating either rule also fails DAO initialization with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

methods.name: impl
methods.signature: @SuppressWarnings("rawtypes") Class<? extends Jdbc.Handler<? extends DaoBase>> impl() default EmptyHandler.class
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the handler implementation class.
methods.returns: the handler class, defaults to {@link EmptyHandler} (no-op)
contract: The class must implement {@link Jdbc.Handler} with the appropriate DAO type parameter: the proxy is passed to its typed {@code beforeInvoke} / {@code afterInvoke} methods, so a handler typed for one DAO interface fails with {@code ClassCastException} when applied to another DAO type.
A handler shared by several DAO types should be typed for a common supertype such as {@code DaoBase<?, ?>} .

If no instance is already registered, the class must be concrete and have a usable no-argument constructor; invalid construction requirements fail with {@code IllegalArgumentException} , while constructor or reflective-access failures can propagate other runtime exceptions.
It runs only if this handler's {@code beforeInvoke()} completed normally, including when a later handler's {@code beforeInvoke()} fails.
When the invocation or a {@code beforeInvoke()} call fails, that failure remains primary while distinct {@code afterInvoke()} failures are attached as suppressed exceptions.

Example handler implementation: 

 {@code public class SecurityHandler implements Jdbc.Handler { @Override public void beforeInvoke(UserDao proxy, Object[] args, Tuple3>, Class> methodSignature) { // Check user permissions if (!hasPermission(methodSignature._1)) { throw new SecurityException("Access denied"); } } @Override public void afterInvoke(Object result, UserDao proxy, Object[] args, Tuple3>, Class> methodSignature) { // Can filter or log results filterSensitiveData(result); } } }

methods.name: filter
methods.signature: String[] filter() default { ".*" }
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies filter patterns for methods when the annotation is applied at the class level.
methods.returns: array of filter patterns (default matches all methods)
contract: Specifies filter patterns for methods when the annotation is applied at the class level.
Each entry matches when the method name starts with that entry (case-insensitive) or when the entry matches the full method name as a regular expression.
Multiple patterns are combined with OR logic \u2014 a method is intercepted if it matches at least one entry.
This filter is ignored when the annotation is applied at the method level.

methods.name: externalCallsOnly
methods.signature: boolean externalCallsOnly() default false
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies whether this handler should only be applied to external invocations of the DAO.
methods.returns: {@code true} if handler only applies to external calls, {@code false} (default) otherwise
contract: Specifies whether this handler should only be applied to external invocations of the DAO.
When {@code true} , the handler will not be triggered for internal method calls within the DAO.
This is useful for handlers that should only apply when the DAO is called from outside code, not when DAO methods call each other internally.

More precisely, a call counts as internal when it is made on the same thread while another DAO method that has at least one {@code @Handler} applied is still executing — on this DAO or on any other DAO proxy.

types.name: Handlers
types.javadoc_summary: Container annotation for multiple {@link Handler} declarations on the same DAO method or type.

methods.name: value
methods.signature: Handler[] value()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the array of {@link Handler} annotations contained in this list.
methods.returns: the array of {@link Handler} annotations contained in this list
contract: When multiple handlers are applied to a DAO or method, they form a chain of interceptors.

Usage Examples: 

 {@code // Accessing Handlers programmatically via reflection Handlers handlers = MyDao.class.getAnnotation(Handlers.class); if (handlers != null) { for (Handler handler : handlers.value()) { System.out.println("Handler impl: " + handler.impl()); System.out.println("Filter: " + Arrays.toString(handler.filter())); } } // Multiple handlers are automatically wrapped in Handlers @Handler(impl = LoggingHandler.class) @Handler(impl = SecurityHandler.class) @Handler(impl = CacheHandler.class) public interface UserDao extends CrudDao { // The compiler wraps these in a Handlers annotation } }

This element is mandatory and has no default value.
When the compiler synthesizes the container from repeated {@link Handler @Handler} annotations it populates this array.
An explicit container must supply the array, but Java permits it to be empty; an empty container simply installs no handlers.

types.name: MappedByKey
types.javadoc_summary: Transforms query results into a Map structure where each result row is keyed by a specified field.

methods.name: value
methods.signature: String value() default ""
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the target-entity property name to use as the map key.
methods.returns: the field name to use as map key, or empty string to fall back to the entity's id property
contract: If left empty, the framework falls back to the target entity's id property name (the first id property when the entity has a composite id); a DAO whose entity has no id property then fails initialization with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

The resolved name must be a readable property of the DAO's target entity class, and the method's key type must accept that property's type; otherwise DAO initialization fails with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

methods.name: mapClass
methods.signature: @SuppressWarnings("rawtypes") Class<? extends Map> mapClass() default HashMap.class
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the Map implementation class to use for the result.
methods.returns: the {@code Map} implementation class to instantiate; defaults to {@link HashMap}
contract: The class must be concrete, have a no-argument constructor, and be assignable to the DAO method's declared return type; each of those is checked at DAO initialization time and a violation fails with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

For example, a method returning {@code LinkedHashMap} must explicitly select {@code LinkedHashMap.class} ; the default {@link HashMap} is only compatible with return types that can accept a {@code HashMap} , such as {@code Map} or {@code HashMap} .

types.name: MergedById
types.javadoc_summary: Merges multiple result rows into single entities based on ID fields.

methods.name: value
methods.signature: String value() default ""
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the property name(s) whose values identify rows to merge.
methods.returns: comma-separated list of property names to merge by, or empty string to use the entity's id property(ies)
contract: This is optional when merging by the entity's declared id: left empty, the framework falls back to the property names annotated with {@code @Id} on the target entity (or, when combined with {@link MappedByKey} , to that annotation's key).

When {@code @MergedById} and {@link MappedByKey} are combined, an explicit {@code @MergedById} value must name exactly the single property that {@code @MappedByKey} resolves to (its explicit value, or the entity's first id property when that value is empty); otherwise DAO initialization fails with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

types.name: NonDBOperation
types.javadoc_summary: Marks methods in DAO interfaces that should not be treated as database operations.

types.name: OutParameter
types.javadoc_summary: Declares an {@code OUT} or {@code INOUT} parameter for a stored-procedure DAO method.

methods.name: name
methods.signature: String name() default ""
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the name of the output parameter.
methods.returns: the parameter name; empty string when {@link #position()} is used instead
contract: Exactly one of {@code name} or {@code position} must be specified for a given {@code @OutParameter} ; supplying both, or neither, fails with {@code UnsupportedOperationException} at DAO initialization time.
Named parameters are generally preferred for readability and maintainability when the JDBC driver and procedure support them.
The parameter name should match the name used in the stored procedure call syntax.

methods.name: position
methods.signature: int position() default -1
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the position of the output parameter.
methods.returns: the parameter position (1-based); {@code -1} (default) when {@link #name()} is used instead
contract: Exactly one of {@code name} or {@code position} must be specified for a given {@code @OutParameter} (supplying both, or neither, fails with {@code UnsupportedOperationException} at DAO initialization time).

methods.name: sqlType
methods.signature: int sqlType()
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the SQL type of the output parameter.
methods.returns: the SQL type code, normally a constant from {@link java.sql.Types}
contract: The framework forwards the value unchanged, so a vendor-specific integer type code may also be used when the JDBC driver supports it.

Common SQL types include:

  • {@link Types#VARCHAR} - String values
  • {@link Types#INTEGER} - Integer values
  • {@link Types#DECIMAL} or {@link Types#NUMERIC} - Decimal numbers
  • {@link Types#DATE} , {@link Types#TIME} , {@link Types#TIMESTAMP} - Date/time values
  • {@link Types#BOOLEAN} - Boolean values
  • {@link Types#CLOB} - Character large objects
  • {@link Types#BLOB} - Binary large objects

The SQL type must match the actual type of the output parameter in the stored procedure.

Usage Examples: 

 {@code @OutParameter(name = "message", sqlType = Types.VARCHAR) @OutParameter(name = "count", sqlType = Types.INTEGER) @OutParameter(name = "amount", sqlType = Types.DECIMAL) @OutParameter(name = "processDate", sqlType = Types.TIMESTAMP) @OutParameter(name = "isActive", sqlType = Types.BOOLEAN) }

This element has no default value and must be specified for every {@code @OutParameter} .

types.name: OutParameters
types.javadoc_summary: Container annotation for repeatable {@link OutParameter} declarations on a single stored-procedure DAO method.

methods.name: value
methods.signature: OutParameter[] value()
methods.javadoc_summary: The array of {@link OutParameter} annotations contained in this list.
methods.returns: the contained {@link OutParameter} annotations
contract: This array is automatically populated when using multiple {@link OutParameter} annotations on a method via the {@link java.lang.annotation.Repeatable} mechanism; direct use of {@code @OutParameters} is rarely needed.

types.name: PerfLog
types.javadoc_summary: Enables SQL and DAO-method performance logging for the annotated method (or for the DAO type, with optional {@link #filter()} matching).

methods.name: maxSqlLogLength
methods.signature: int maxSqlLogLength() default JdbcUtil.DEFAULT_MAX_SQL_LOG_LENGTH
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the maximum length of SQL statements in performance logs.
methods.returns: the maximum number of characters to include from SQL statements in logs; defaults to {@link JdbcUtil#DEFAULT_MAX_SQL_LOG_LENGTH} (1024 characters)
contract: This is useful for maintaining readable logs when dealing with complex queries or queries with large parameter lists.

methods.name: sqlPerfLogThresholdMillis
methods.signature: long sqlPerfLogThresholdMillis() default JdbcUtil.DEFAULT_SQL_PERF_LOG_THRESHOLD_MILLIS
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the minimum execution time threshold (in milliseconds) for logging SQL performance.
methods.returns: the minimum execution time in milliseconds for SQL logging; defaults to {@link JdbcUtil#DEFAULT_SQL_PERF_LOG_THRESHOLD_MILLIS} (1000 ms)

methods.name: daoMethodPerfLogThresholdMillis
methods.signature: long daoMethodPerfLogThresholdMillis() default JdbcUtil.DEFAULT_DAO_METHOD_PERF_LOG_THRESHOLD_MILLIS
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the minimum execution time threshold (in milliseconds) for logging DAO method performance.
methods.returns: the minimum execution time in milliseconds for DAO operation logging; defaults to {@link JdbcUtil#DEFAULT_DAO_METHOD_PERF_LOG_THRESHOLD_MILLIS} (3000 ms)

methods.name: filter
methods.signature: String[] filter() default { ".*" }
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the type-level method-name filter.
methods.returns: array of filter patterns (default matches all methods)
contract: Each entry matches when the method name starts with it (ignoring case), or when it matches the full method name as a regular expression.

types.name: PrefixFieldMapping
types.javadoc_summary: Maps prefixed column aliases to nested target paths during row-to-bean mapping.

methods.name: value
methods.signature: String value() default ""
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the mapping between column prefixes and object field paths.
methods.returns: the comma-separated {@code prefix=fieldPath} mapping string; empty (default) means no prefix mapping is applied
contract: • Column-alias syntax (in the SQL query): each matching column alias must be of the form {@code prefix.columnName} , i.e.

Resolution rules:

  • Each {@code prefix} must match the leading segment (before the dot) of the column aliases used in the query (e.g., the prefix {@code addr} matches the alias {@code addr.street} )
  • The {@code prefix.} portion is stripped from the alias, and the remaining column name is mapped onto the configured {@code fieldPath} target
  • Columns whose aliases have no matching prefix are mapped normally

Example mappings: 

 {@code // Simple prefix mapping @PrefixFieldMapping("addr=address") // addr.street -> address.street // addr.city -> address.city // Multiple prefix mappings @PrefixFieldMapping("u=user, o=order, p=payment") // u.name -> user.name // o.id -> order.id // p.amount -> payment.amount // Nested field mapping @PrefixFieldMapping("bill=billing.address, ship=shipping.address") // bill.street -> billing.address.street // ship.street -> shipping.address.street }

types.name: Query
types.javadoc_summary: Declares how a DAO method should execute SQL.

methods.name: value
methods.signature: String[] value() default {}
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the inline SQL statement(s) to execute.
methods.returns: inline SQL statement lines; empty by default when using {@link #id()}
contract: An ordinary abstract DAO method must specify exactly one entry; supplying more than one entry (across {@code value} and {@link #id()} ) fails DAO initialization — with {@link IllegalArgumentException} when both {@code value} and {@link #id()} are supplied, or with {@code UnsupportedOperationException} when multiple entries are declared on an abstract method.

When the annotated method is a {@code default} method whose last parameter is a {@code String[]} , all entries from {@code value} and {@link #id()} are collected, dereferenced through the SQL mapper if applicable, and passed to that {@code String[]} parameter at runtime.
The caller must leave that parameter empty; passing any SQL in it fails the call with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

The SQL can include:

  • Named parameters using {@code :paramName} syntax for value binding
  • Template variables using {@code {variableName}} syntax (defined by {@link SqlFragment} or {@link SqlFragmentList} ); set {@link #fragmentsContainNamedParameters()} to {@code true} if the replaced fragments contain named parameters
  • Standard SQL features like JOINs, subqueries, CTEs (Common Table Expressions), window functions, etc.

• Database-specific SQL extensions and functions

    • Named parameter examples: 

     {@code // Simple parameter binding @Query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > :minAge") List findByAge(@Bind("minAge") int minAge) throws SQLException; // Multiple parameters @Query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE age BETWEEN :minAge AND :maxAge") List findByAgeRange(@Bind("minAge") int min, @Bind("maxAge") int max) throws SQLException; // Nested property paths require a single unannotated bean parameter // (filter.getUser().getId() and filter.getStatus() supply the values) @Query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = :user.id AND status = :status") List findOrders(OrderFilter filter) throws SQLException; // IN clause with collection (uses {ids} template variable expanded via @BindList) @Query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN ({ids})") List findByIds(@BindList("ids") List ids) throws SQLException; }

    Complex SQL examples: 

     {@code // JOIN with aggregation @Query("SELECT u.*, COUNT(o.id) as order_count " + "FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id " + "WHERE u.created_date > :startDate " + "GROUP BY u.id HAVING COUNT(o.id) > :minOrders") List findUserStats(@Bind("startDate") Date startDate, @Bind("minOrders") int minOrders) throws SQLException; // Common Table Expression (CTE) @Query("WITH recent_orders AS ( " + " SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) as order_count " + " FROM orders WHERE order_date > :since " + " GROUP BY user_id " + ") " + "SELECT u.*, ro.order_count " + "FROM users u JOIN recent_orders ro ON u.id = ro.user_id") List findActiveUserSummary(@Bind("since") Date since) throws SQLException; // Window function @Query("SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) as rank " + "FROM employees WHERE department = :dept") List rankEmployeesByDepartment(@Bind("dept") String department) throws SQLException; }

    A single {@code value} entry that contains no whitespace and equals an id defined through {@link SqlSource} , a {@link SqlScript} field, or the SQL mapper supplied when the DAO is created is treated as that id: the referenced SQL, and any mapper attributes of that id (timeout, fetch size, batch size), are used instead of the literal text.
Note: On an abstract method exactly one of {@code value} or {@link #id()} must be non-empty; specifying both or neither causes initialization to fail with an {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

methods.name: id
methods.signature: String[] id() default {}
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies SQL statement identifier lines referencing SQL defined in an external SQL mapper (see {@link SqlSource} ) or in a {@link SqlScript} field on the DAO.
methods.returns: SQL statement id lines resolved through the SQL mapper or a {@link SqlScript} field; empty by default when using {@link #value()}
contract: Each id entry must be a valid Java identifier as per {@link RegExUtil#JAVA_IDENTIFIER_MATCHER} , and must resolve to a non-empty SQL statement; an id that is not a Java identifier, or that no {@link SqlSource} entry, no {@link SqlScript} field and no SQL mapper supplied when the DAO is created defines, fails DAO initialization with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

An ordinary abstract DAO method must specify exactly one entry; supplying more than one entry (across {@link #value()} and {@code id} ) fails DAO initialization — with {@link IllegalArgumentException} when both {@link #value()} and {@code id} are supplied, or with {@code UnsupportedOperationException} when multiple entries are declared on an abstract method.

When the annotated method is a {@code default} method whose last parameter is a {@code String[]} , all entries from {@link #value()} and {@code id} are collected, dereferenced through the SQL mapper if applicable, and passed to that {@code String[]} parameter at runtime.
The caller must leave that parameter empty; passing any SQL in it fails the call with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

// }

Note: On an abstract method exactly one of {@link #value()} or {@code id} must be non-empty; specifying both or neither causes initialization to fail with an {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

methods.name: op
methods.signature: QueryOperation op() default QueryOperation.DEFAULT
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the operation type for this query.
methods.returns: the operation type, defaults to {@link QueryOperation#DEFAULT}
contract:
The operation type influences:

  • Result set processing strategy
  • Return type handling and conversion
  • Performance optimizations applied by the framework
  • Expected behavior for edge cases (e.g., empty results)

Common operation types:

  • {@link QueryOperation#DEFAULT} - Framework determines operation based on SQL and return type (recommended for most cases)
  • {@link QueryOperation#list} - Returns all results as a List
  • {@link QueryOperation#stream} - (Deprecated) Returns results as an Abacus {@link com.landawn.abacus.util.stream.Stream} ; prefer {@link QueryOperation#DEFAULT} with that return type
  • {@link QueryOperation#findFirst} - Returns the first result (wrapped in an Abacus {@link com.landawn.abacus.util.u.Optional} when the method has that return type, otherwise the bare value or the return type's empty/default value when none)
  • {@link QueryOperation#findOnlyOne} - Returns at most one result (wrapped in an Abacus {@link com.landawn.abacus.util.u.Optional} when the method has that return type, otherwise the bare value or the return type's default value when none); throws {@code DuplicateResultException} if more than one is found
  • {@link QueryOperation#exists} - Returns boolean indicating if any results exist
  • {@link QueryOperation#queryForSingle} - Returns a single scalar value
  • {@link QueryOperation#queryForUnique} - Returns at most one scalar value using the declared optional/nullable wrapper, or the bare value and its type's default value when no row exists; throws {@code DuplicateResultException} if more than one row is found
  • {@link QueryOperation#update} - Executes a non-INSERT data-modification statement and returns its row count
  • {@link QueryOperation#largeUpdate} - For updates affecting potentially more than {@code Integer.MAX_VALUE} rows

Usage Examples: 

 {@code // Existence check @Query(value = "SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE email = :email", op = QueryOperation.exists) boolean emailExists(@Bind("email") String email) throws SQLException; // Single scalar value @Query(value = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE active = true", op = QueryOperation.queryForSingle) long countActiveUsers() throws SQLException; // First result from ordered query @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY created_date DESC", op = QueryOperation.findFirst) com.landawn.abacus.util.u.Optional findLatestUser() throws SQLException; // At most one match (throws DuplicateResultException if more than one matches; null if none) @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :id", op = QueryOperation.findOnlyOne) User getUserById(@Bind("id") Long id) throws SQLException; // An Abacus Stream return type makes the framework stream automatically @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM large_table", fetchSize = 1000) com.landawn.abacus.util.stream.Stream streamAllRecords(); // Explicit update operation @Query(value = "DELETE FROM audit_logs WHERE created_date < :cutoff", op = QueryOperation.update) int purgeOldLogs(@Bind("cutoff") Date cutoff) throws SQLException; }

When to specify explicitly:

  • For existence checks: use {@code QueryOperation.exists} for performance
  • For scalar aggregates: use {@code QueryOperation.queryForSingle}
  • When you need strict validation: use {@code QueryOperation.findOnlyOne}
  • For large result sets: return an Abacus {@link com.landawn.abacus.util.stream.Stream} with an appropriate fetch size (the framework streams automatically)

Note: In most cases, {@link QueryOperation#DEFAULT} is sufficient as the framework intelligently determines the appropriate operation based on the SQL statement type and method return type.

methods.name: procedure
methods.signature: boolean procedure() default false
methods.javadoc_summary: Indicates whether the SQL statement is a stored procedure call.
methods.returns: {@code true} if the SQL is a stored procedure call; {@code false} (default) otherwise
contract: When {@code true} , the framework treats the SQL as a callable statement and handles input/output parameters accordingly.

A single bean, record or {@link com.landawn.abacus.util.EntityId} parameter cannot supply procedure parameters and causes DAO initialization to throw {@link UnsupportedOperationException} , including when it is annotated with {@code @Bind} in positional ( {@code ?} ) SQL.

@Query(value = "{call calculate_bonus(?, ?, ?)}", procedure = true, op = QueryOperation.executeAndGetOutParameters) @OutParameter(position = 3, sqlType = Types.DECIMAL) // bonus (OUT) Jdbc.OutParamResult calculateBonus(long employeeId, int performanceScore) throws SQLException; // BigDecimal bonus = dao.calculateBonus(1L, 95).getOutParamValue(3); }

When to use:

  • Calling stored procedures or functions in the database
  • When the SQL syntax follows the callable statement format (e.g., {@code {call procedure_name(?, ?)}} )
  • When using output parameters that need to be registered and retrieved

Procedure-only features: {@link OutParameter @OutParameter} / {@link OutParameters @OutParameters} and the {@link QueryOperation#listAll} , {@link QueryOperation#queryAll} , {@link QueryOperation#streamAll} and {@link QueryOperation#executeAndGetOutParameters} operations all require {@code procedure = true} ; using any of them while this element is {@code false} fails DAO initialization with {@code UnsupportedOperationException} .

methods.name: batch
methods.signature: boolean batch() default false
methods.javadoc_summary: Indicates whether this query should be executed as a batch operation.
methods.returns: {@code true} for batch operations; {@code false} (default) for single operations
contract: Indicates whether this query should be executed as a batch operation.
When {@code true} , the method should accept collection-type parameters and execute the query multiple times with different parameter sets in a single batch for better performance.

Batch operations significantly improve performance when executing the same SQL statement multiple times with different parameters by:

  • Reducing network round trips to the database
  • Allowing the database to optimize execution plans
  • Minimizing parsing and compilation overhead
  • Enabling better resource utilization

When to use batch operations:

  • Inserting multiple records (most common use case)
  • Updating multiple records with different values
  • Deleting multiple records based on different criteria
  • Any scenario where the same SQL runs many times with different parameters

Basic batch insert examples: 

 {@code // Batch insert with entity list: the single Collection parameter supplies one entity per batch row @Query(value = "INSERT INTO users (name, email, status) " + "VALUES (:name, :email, :status)", batch = true) List batchInsertUsers(List users) throws SQLException; // Returns the generated keys (or declare void if they are not needed) }

Batch update/delete examples: 

 {@code // Batch update with entity list @Query(value = "UPDATE users SET status = :status WHERE id = :id", batch = true) int batchUpdateStatus(List users) throws SQLException; // Returns the sum of positive row counts reported by the driver // Batch delete: for positional SQL each element of the Collection is one row's value // (or an Object[]/List of values for multi-parameter SQL) @Query(value = "DELETE FROM temp_records WHERE id = ?", batch = true) int batchDelete(List ids) throws SQLException; }

Advanced batch examples: 

 {@code // Large batch with custom batch size @Query(value = "INSERT INTO event_log (timestamp, event_type, data) " + "VALUES (:timestamp, :eventType, :data)", batch = true, batchSize = 1000) void batchLogEvents(List events) throws SQLException; // Processes 1000 records per database round trip // Batch with timeout for large operations; the optional second int parameter // overrides batchSize() at call time (0 falls back to the default batch size) @Query(value = "INSERT INTO historical_data (date, metric, value) " + "VALUES (:date, :metric, :value)", batch = true, queryTimeoutSeconds = 300) void importHistoricalData(List rows, int batchSize) throws SQLException; }

Return type requirements:

  • Batch INSERT: {@code void} , or {@code List} to receive the generated keys
  • Batch UPDATE/DELETE: {@code int} / {@code Integer} , {@code long} / {@code Long} , {@code boolean} / {@code Boolean} or {@code void} \u2014 positive affected-row counts are summed across all batch rows (a per-row {@code int[]} result is not supported).

JDBC sentinel values such as {@link java.sql.Statement#SUCCESS_NO_INFO} do not contribute to the sum; a boolean result reports whether that sum is positive, so it can be {@code false} even when the driver reports successful execution without row counts.

Performance considerations:

  • Use {@link #batchSize()} to control how many items are sent per database round trip
  • Larger batch sizes reduce round trips but increase memory usage
  • Optimal batch size depends on network latency, row size, and database configuration
  • Consider database transaction log size and timeout limits
  • Measure with the target driver and database; batching benefits vary with row size, network latency, and driver rewrite behavior

Error handling:

  • If a batch item fails, the driver may report partial execution.

• Use {@link Transactional} when rollback is also required for single-chunk batches
  • Validate data before batching to minimize mid-batch failures

    • Best practices:

    • Use batch operations for bulk data loading and imports
    • Set appropriate {@link #batchSize()} based on your data and environment
    • Use {@link #queryTimeoutSeconds()} for long-running batch operations
    • Monitor memory usage with large batches
    • Consider using transactions to ensure all-or-nothing semantics
    • Validate that each batch row supplies every SQL parameter required by the statement

methods.name: collectionAsSingleParameter
methods.signature: boolean collectionAsSingleParameter() default false
methods.javadoc_summary: Controls whether the sole statement argument is bound once as a single JDBC value instead of being decomposed by the DAO proxy.
methods.returns: {@code true} if the sole statement argument should be bound once as a single value; {@code false} (default) to use the normal positional/batch decomposition rules
contract:
Default behavior ( {@code collectionAsSingleParameter = false} ):

  • A sole, unannotated {@code Collection} or reference array used with positional {@code ?} SQL supplies the individual positional values; primitive arrays are passed as one value unless expanded explicitly with {@link BindList}
  • For batch operations, the outer collection supplies the rows to process

When {@code collectionAsSingleParameter = true} :

  • The collection/array is passed once through {@code PreparedStatement.setObject}
  • The JDBC driver must accept that Java value as one database value, commonly for a database-native array or another driver-specific type

Common use cases: 

 {@code // PostgreSQL array containment operator using one positional JDBC value @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE tags @> ?", collectionAsSingleParameter = true) List findByTags(String[] tags) throws SQLException; // PostgreSQL array equality @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM events WHERE participants = ?", collectionAsSingleParameter = true) List findByExactParticipants(Long[] participants) throws SQLException; // A driver-supported native array/custom type (exact conversion is driver-specific) @Query(value = "UPDATE configs SET options = ?

WHERE name = 'default'", collectionAsSingleParameter = true) int updateDefaultConfigOptions(String[] options) throws SQLException; // Array intersection @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM items WHERE categories && ?", collectionAsSingleParameter = true) List findByCategoryOverlap(String[] categories) throws SQLException; }

Contrast with default behavior: 

 {@code // Variable-length IN expansion is a separate @BindList feature @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN ({ids})") List findByIds(@BindList("ids") List ids) throws SQLException; // Becomes: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (?, ?, ?, ...) // With collectionAsSingleParameter: the array is passed once to one positional placeholder @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ANY(?)", collectionAsSingleParameter = true) List findByIdsArray(Long[] ids) throws SQLException; // PostgreSQL: id = ANY($1) where $1 is an array parameter }

Important notes:

  • The collection/array must be the method's only statement/query parameter, apart from an optional {@code int} batch-size argument for batch methods; fragment and other framework-recognized auxiliary parameters are not statement parameters.

Setting this element on a method with any other number of statement parameters fails DAO initialization with {@code UnsupportedOperationException}
  • For batch methods, each element of the batch collection is bound as one value
  • The JDBC driver and database must support binding the supplied Java collection/array as one value; this option does not call {@code Connection.createArrayOf}
  • Not commonly needed for standard SQL; primarily for database-specific features

methods.name: fragmentsContainNamedParameters
methods.signature: @Beta boolean fragmentsContainNamedParameters() default false
methods.javadoc_summary: Indicates whether the query fragments substituted for {@link SqlFragment} / {@link SqlFragmentList} template variables themselves contain named parameters that must also be parsed and bound.
methods.returns: {@code true} if template variables defined by {@link SqlFragment} or {@link SqlFragmentList} will be replaced with query fragments containing named parameters; {@code false} otherwise
contract: Indicates whether the query fragments substituted for {@link SqlFragment} / {@link SqlFragmentList} template variables themselves contain named parameters that must also be parsed and bound.
Set this to {@code true} when a replaced fragment itself contains named parameters, so the framework parses the merged SQL and binds them as well.

Enabling this flag makes the method a named query even when the static SQL declares no named parameter of its own, so its statement parameters follow the named-binding rules of {@link Bind} and the bound names are verified against the SQL only after the fragments have been expanded.
The static SQL must not rely on positional placeholders: if it declares parameters but none of them is named (only {@code ?} markers), DAO initialization fails with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

methods.name: injectCurrentTimeParameters
methods.signature: @Beta boolean injectCurrentTimeParameters() default false
methods.javadoc_summary: Enables automatic system-time parameter injection for the query.
methods.returns: {@code true} to automatically inject current timestamp as {@code :sysTime} or {@code :now} , and current date as {@code :sysDate} , without requiring them as method parameters; {@code false} (default) for no automatic injection
contract: When {@code true} , the named parameters {@code :now} and {@code :sysTime} are automatically set to the current system timestamp, and the named parameter {@code :sysDate} is automatically set to the current system date, without requiring any of them to be passed as method parameters.

• The value is obtained from the application server's system time, not the database server
  • For database server time, use SQL functions like {@code CURRENT_TIMESTAMP} or {@code NOW()} instead
  • The timestamp format and precision depend on the database column type and JDBC driver
  • Cannot manually override the {@code :now} , {@code :sysTime} , or {@code :sysDate} parameters when this is enabled

    • When not to use this feature:

    • When you need explicit control over the timestamp value
    • When you need database server time instead of application time
    • When the timestamp should be passed in from external sources
    • When you need different timestamps for different parts of a complex operation

methods.name: queryTimeoutSeconds
methods.signature: int queryTimeoutSeconds() default -1
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the query timeout in seconds.
methods.returns: the timeout in seconds, or {@code -1} to leave the statement timeout unchanged
contract:
Setting an appropriate timeout is important for:

  • Preventing resource exhaustion from long-running queries
  • Meeting Service Level Agreement (SLA) requirements
  • Detecting and failing fast on inefficient queries
  • Protecting the application from database performance issues
  • Preventing connection pool starvation

Timeout guidelines (in seconds):

  • {@code -1} (default) - This annotation leaves the statement timeout unchanged
  • {@code 0} - No timeout (wait indefinitely - not recommended)
  • {@code 1-5} - For simple, well-indexed queries that should be very fast
  • {@code 10-30} - For complex queries with joins or aggregations
  • {@code 60+} - For batch operations, data migrations, or reporting queries

Usage Examples: 

 {@code // Quick lookup that should complete fast @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :id", queryTimeoutSeconds = 2) User getUserById(@Bind("id") Long id) throws SQLException; // Complex reporting query @Query(value = "SELECT SUM(amount) FROM sales WHERE sale_month = :month", queryTimeoutSeconds = 60) double getMonthlySalesTotal(@Bind("month") int month) throws SQLException; // Batch operation with generous timeout @Query(value = "INSERT INTO archive SELECT * FROM data WHERE year = :year", queryTimeoutSeconds = 300) void archiveYearData(@Bind("year") int year) throws SQLException; // External API call timeout @Query(value = "SELECT get_external_data(:param)", queryTimeoutSeconds = 10) String callExternalService(@Bind("param") String param) throws SQLException; }

Best practices:

  • Set timeouts based on expected query performance in production
  • Consider network latency and database load
  • Use shorter timeouts for user-facing operations
  • Log timeout exceptions to identify slow queries
  • Review and optimize queries that frequently time out

Note: The actual timeout behavior depends on the JDBC driver implementation.

methods.name: fetchSize
methods.signature: int fetchSize() default -1
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the JDBC fetch size for the query.
methods.returns: the fetch size hint for the JDBC driver; only positive values are forwarded to the statement ( {@code -1} and {@code 0} both leave it unset). When unset, the framework may still apply its own per-operation fetch size for SELECTs (e.g. 1 for find-first/exists style queries, 2 for find-only-one/unique queries, and a large-result configuration for streaming) rather than the raw driver default
contract: The fetch size is a hint to the JDBC driver about the number of rows that should be fetched from the database when more rows are needed.

Higher values significantly improve performance for large result sets
  • SQL Server: Adaptive fetch size based on packet size

    • Important notes:

    • Fetch size is a hint; drivers may ignore or adjust it
    • Very large fetch sizes can cause OutOfMemoryError if rows are large
    • Optimal fetch size depends on network latency, row size, and available memory
    • For Abacus {@link com.landawn.abacus.util.stream.Stream} return types, fetch size is a buffering hint; actual cursor and prefetch behavior remains driver-specific
    • Profile and test with realistic data to find optimal values
    • Consider using different fetch sizes for different environments (dev vs.

methods.name: batchSize
methods.signature: int batchSize() default JdbcUtil.DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the number of items to process in each database round trip for batch operations.
methods.returns: the number of items to process per batch, defaults to {@link JdbcUtil#DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE}
contract: Only applicable when {@link #batch()} is {@code true} .

batchSize = 100 - Total database round trips: 10,000 / 100 = 100 trips - Each trip processes 100 INSERT statements - Memory per trip: ~100 × row size - More round trips but less memory per trip

Factors to consider when choosing batch size:

  • Row size: Larger rows require smaller batch sizes to avoid memory issues
  • Network latency: High latency benefits from larger batches
  • Database limits: Some databases have maximum transaction sizes or statement counts
  • Available memory: Limited memory requires smaller batches
  • Concurrent operations: Consider memory usage across all concurrent operations
  • Error handling: Smaller batches may be easier to retry on partial failures

Database-specific considerations:

  • PostgreSQL: Can handle very large batches efficiently; consider 1000-5000
  • MySQL: May have max_allowed_packet limit; typically 500-2000
  • Oracle: Efficient with batches of 100-1000
  • SQL Server: Generally efficient with 500-1000

Memory usage estimation: 

 Approximate memory per batch = batchSize × averageRowSize × 2 (×2 accounts for driver buffering and object overhead) Example calculations: - Small rows (100 bytes), batchSize 5000 \u2192 ~1MB per batch - Medium rows (1KB), batchSize 1000 \u2192 ~2MB per batch - Large rows (10KB), batchSize 100 \u2192 ~2MB per batch - Very large rows (100KB), batchSize 10 \u2192 ~2MB per batch

Best practices:

  • Start with the default and measure performance
  • Profile with realistic data volumes and row sizes
  • Monitor memory usage under load
  • Consider different values for different environments (dev vs.

prod)
  • Document the rationale for non-default batch sizes
  • Test with edge cases (very small and very large datasets)

    • Common anti-patterns to avoid:

    • Using batch size of 1 (defeats the purpose of batching)
    • Using extremely large batch sizes without memory testing
    • Ignoring database-specific limitations
    • Not adjusting batch size when row size changes significantly

methods.returns: array of filter patterns for method names that should trigger cache refresh; the default targets common write methods such as {@code update} , {@code delete} , {@code deleteById} , {@code insert} , {@code save} , {@code add} , {@code remove} , {@code upsert} , {@code execute} and their {@code batch*} variants
contract: Each entry matches when the method name starts with that entry (case-insensitive) or when the entry matches the full method name as a regular expression.

types.name: SqlFragment
types.javadoc_summary: Performs SQL template substitution for one query fragment.

methods.name: value
methods.signature: String value() default ""
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the name of the query template variable that this parameter replaces.
methods.returns: the template-variable name; empty means use the method parameter name (requires {@code -parameters} )
contract: If empty (the default), the actual method parameter name is used; this requires compiling with the {@code -parameters} javac flag, otherwise initialization fails with {@code UnsupportedOperationException} .

Example: 

 {@code @Query("SELECT * FROM {schema}.{table} WHERE id = :id") User findById( @SqlFragment("schema") String schemaName, @SqlFragment("table") String tableName, @Bind("id") long id ) throws SQLException; }

Using the method parameter name (requires {@code -parameters} ): 

 {@code @Query("SELECT {columns} FROM users") List> findWithColumns(@SqlFragment String columns) throws SQLException; // The parameter name "columns" is used as the template-variable name }

The resolved name must correspond to a {@code {name}} token in the surrounding {@link Query @Query} SQL, and each fragment parameter on a method must target a distinct token; a name with no matching token, and two parameters resolving to the same token, both fail DAO initialization with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

types.javadoc_summary: Joins a collection or array of strings into a comma-separated SQL fragment that replaces the {@code {name}} token in the surrounding {@link Query @Query} SQL.

methods.returns: the template-variable name; empty means use the method parameter name (requires {@code -parameters} )
contract: If empty (the default), the actual method parameter name is used; this requires compiling with the {@code -parameters} javac flag, otherwise initialization fails with {@code UnsupportedOperationException} .

Usage Examples: 

 {@code // Explicit name @Query("SELECT {cols} FROM users") List findWithColumns(@SqlFragmentList("cols") List columnList) throws SQLException; // Using the method parameter name (requires '-parameters') @Query("SELECT {columns} FROM users") List findWithColumns(@SqlFragmentList List columns) throws SQLException; }

The resolved name must correspond to a {@code {name}} token in the surrounding {@link Query @Query} SQL; a name with no matching token fails DAO initialization with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

types.name: SqlLogEnabled
types.javadoc_summary: Toggles whether SQL statements are logged for a DAO method (or all matching methods on a DAO type).

methods.name: value
methods.signature: boolean value() default true
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies whether SQL logging is enabled or disabled.
methods.returns: {@code true} to enable SQL logging, {@code false} to disable it
contract: When set to {@code true} , SQL statements will be logged for the annotated scope; when set to {@code false} , SQL logging is disabled for that scope.
When no {@code @SqlLogEnabled} is present at all, logging follows the current thread's setting configured on {@link JdbcUtil} .

methods.name: maxSqlLogLength
methods.signature: int maxSqlLogLength() default JdbcUtil.DEFAULT_MAX_SQL_LOG_LENGTH
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the maximum length of SQL statements in logs.
methods.returns: the maximum number of characters to include from SQL statements in logs; defaults to {@link JdbcUtil#DEFAULT_MAX_SQL_LOG_LENGTH} (1024)
contract: This setting only has an effect when SQL logging is enabled via {@link #value()} .

This is particularly useful when dealing with:

  • Large INSERT statements with many values
  • Complex queries with multiple joins
  • Queries with large IN clauses
  • Statements with embedded large text or binary data

Usage Examples: 

 {@code @Query(value = "INSERT INTO data_table (payload) VALUES (:payload)", batch = true) @SqlLogEnabled(maxSqlLogLength = 500) void insertBatchData(List largeDataset) throws SQLException; @Query("SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS total FROM reports GROUP BY department") @SqlLogEnabled(maxSqlLogLength = 2048) // Allow longer logs for complex queries List generateComplexReport() throws SQLException; }

methods.name: filter
methods.signature: String[] filter() default { ".*" }
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the type-level method-name filter.
methods.returns: array of filter patterns (default matches all methods)
contract: Each entry matches when the method name starts with it (ignoring case), or when it matches the full method name as a regular expression.

types.name: SqlScript
types.javadoc_summary: Marks a {@code static final String} field as a named SQL script \u2014 an inline alternative to pulling SQL from an external mapper via {@link SqlSource} .

methods.name: id
methods.signature: String id() default ""
methods.javadoc_summary: Supplies an optional identifier that overrides the annotated field name when the SQL is registered.
methods.returns: the identifier used by {@link Query#id()} ; empty means the annotated field name is used
contract: Supplies an optional identifier that overrides the annotated field name when the SQL is registered.
When left empty, the declaration name (for example {@code sql_listUserWithBiggerId} ) becomes the key.

Usage Examples: 

 {@code @SqlScript(id = "sql_listUserWithBiggerId") static final String listUserWithBiggerId = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id > :id"; }

When supplied, the id must be a non-empty, valid Java identifier, unique among all {@link SqlScript} fields on the DAO, and must not collide with any id loaded via {@link SqlSource} ; otherwise DAO initialization fails with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

types.name: SqlSource
types.javadoc_summary: Associates a DAO interface with an external SQL mapper resource.

methods.name: value
methods.signature: String value() default ""
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the path to the SQL mapper XML file.
methods.returns: the SQL-mapper location passed to {@code SqlMapper.loadFrom} ; empty (default) means no external mapper is associated with this DAO
contract: After surrounding whitespace is trimmed, the location is passed to {@code SqlMapper.loadFrom(...)} at DAO initialization time and should include the file extension.

Common conventions:

  • Place mapper files in a resources directory mirroring the package structure
  • Name mapper files after the DAO interface (e.g., UserDao.xml for UserDao interface)
  • Use a dedicated directory like "sql/" or "mappers/" for organization

Example paths: 

 {@code @SqlSource("sql/UserDao.xml") // In sql directory @SqlSource("com/example/dao/UserDao.xml") // Package-based path @SqlSource("mappers/user-queries.xml") // Custom naming }

Every SQL id loaded from this resource must be unique across the mapper and any {@link SqlScript} fields declared on the same DAO; a collision fails DAO initialization with {@code IllegalArgumentException} .

types.name: Transactional
types.javadoc_summary: Declares transaction settings for a DAO method managed by the Abacus JDBC proxy.

methods.name: propagation
methods.signature: Propagation propagation() default Propagation.REQUIRED
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the transaction propagation behavior.
methods.returns: the configured propagation behavior; defaults to {@link Propagation#REQUIRED}
contract:
Common propagation behaviors:

  • {@link Propagation#REQUIRED} (default) - Join existing transaction or create new one
  • {@link Propagation#REQUIRES_NEW} - Always create a new transaction
  • {@link Propagation#SUPPORTS} - Use transaction if exists, otherwise non-transactional
  • {@link Propagation#MANDATORY} - Must execute within existing transaction
  • {@link Propagation#NOT_SUPPORTED} - Execute non-transactionally, suspend existing
  • {@link Propagation#NEVER} - Execute non-transactionally, fail if transaction exists

The two context-demanding policies are enforced before an uncached method execution, before the method body runs, and both report an {@link IllegalStateException} : {@link Propagation#MANDATORY} when the calling thread has no active transaction on the DAO's {@code DataSource} , and {@link Propagation#NEVER} when it does.

methods.name: isolationLevel
methods.signature: IsolationLevel isolationLevel() default IsolationLevel.DEFAULT
methods.javadoc_summary: Specifies the transaction isolation level.
methods.returns: the configured isolation level; defaults to {@link IsolationLevel#DEFAULT}

params.name: entity
params.javadoc: the entity to insert or update

throws.condition: if {@code entity} is {@code null} or {@code matchPropNames} is {@code null} or empty, or if any name in {@code matchPropNames} is not a readable property of the entity class, or an existing row is updated and {@code entity} has a property the loaded entity does not
if Spring connection acquisition is enabled and cannot obtain a required database connection
if acquiring a connection fails, or looking up an existing row or executing the required INSERT or UPDATE statement fails
if more than one record matches the specified {@code matchPropNames}
if an existing row is updated and the loaded class is an immutable bean

contract: Executes an upsert operation: inserts the entity if no record matches the unique properties, otherwise updates the existing record.

methods.javadoc_summary: Executes an upsert operation: inserts the entity if no record matches the condition, otherwise updates the existing record.
methods.returns: the saved entity (the input entity if it was newly inserted; otherwise the merged existing entity that was updated)
contract: Executes an upsert operation: inserts the entity if no record matches the condition, otherwise updates the existing record.

When a record is found, the non- {@code null} non-id properties of {@code entity} are copied into the loaded record before it is updated; a {@code null} property keeps the existing value, so an upsert cannot clear a column to {@code NULL} .
